Chapter 1: When the World Feels Tilted—The Start of an Uncertain Journey
Have you ever had one of those moments when it suddenly feels like life’s rules have changed overnight? Where the world you thought you knew just... stops making sense? For some people, that shift sneaks in quietly. You don’t even notice it at first—until one day, something happens that throws everything into sharp focus.
Back in the late 1960s, there was a young woman living right in that in-between. She was barely out of her teens, in a world that seemed to expect her to move forward without missing a beat—college, career, all those next steps. But deep down, she felt lost, unable to keep up with the certainty everyone else seemed to have.
It all started with a simple trip to the doctor. She’d been feeling off for months—nights without sleep, a mind that just wouldn’t slow down, and a constant sense that something was wrong, even if she couldn’t say exactly what. After a short talk, the doctor suggested she needed some “rest.” It sounded gentle enough, right? But that word carried a weight she wasn’t prepared for. Within hours, she found herself on the way to a psychiatric hospital. Her life, suddenly, was split into a before and after.
The hospital was like stepping into another world. The air felt dense, the routines strict and unyielding. Locked doors, endless white walls, and a steady hum of activity that never quite drowned out the tension underneath. The staff moved with a kind of practiced calm, their faces giving nothing away. For her, it was both a place of safety and a place of confinement—a contradiction she’d wrestle with for almost two years.
Inside, she met others who were also trying to find their footing. Some had been there for months, others for years. Each person carried their own story, their own struggle. There was a young woman who barely spoke, using silence as a shield; another who paced the halls over and over, as if walking a straight line could bring order to chaos; and someone else who clung tightly to daily routines, taking comfort in the predictability of meals and medication.
Slowly, days settled into a rhythm—group therapy, art classes, visits from family who often seemed more confused than supportive. She became both an observer and a participant, trying to figure out where she fit in this strange new world. What stood out was how quickly labels got thrown around—words like “borderline,” “depressed,” “schizophrenic.” Just a single word could change how others looked at her... and even how she started to see herself.
Over time, it became clear that the hospital wasn’t just about treatment. It was a kind of limbo. Time moved differently there—not by seasons or milestones, but by tiny changes: a new roommate, a shift in medication, a rare trip outside. The outside world started to fade, its demands and expectations drifting further away each day.
But even in this closed-off place, she found moments of connection. Friendships formed between people who all felt out of place. They learned to navigate the ups and downs together—finding humor in the weirdness and comfort in shared experience. Through these relationships, she started to realize that healing didn’t mean going back to some perfect version of “normal,” but learning how to live with uncertainty.
And so, her journey into the unknown had only just begun. The lines between sanity and illness, freedom and confinement, self and diagnosis, kept blurring. The hospital was both a refuge and a prison—a place where searching for meaning took on an urgency she’d never known before.
